s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time figure; Anduril marked at the 61B USD valuation set in its May 2026 round
did: Built the first Oculus Rift VR headset in his parents Long Beach garage at 16, sold Oculus to Facebook for 2 billion dollars in 2014, then founded Anduril in 2017 to sell autonomous towers, drones and the Lattice command software to the Pentagon on a fixed-price product model.
why: Defense primes bill cost-plus on decade-long programs, so nobody funded hardware before a contract existed. Anduril built products on venture money first and sold them finished, which let it undercut program-of-record timelines and win border and counter-drone work the primes could not bid fast enough.
obst: Fired from Facebook in 2017 after a political donation became public, which he called a firing over politics; Anduril then spent years being told by investors that selling to the Pentagon was uninvestable and by the Pentagon that a startup could not hold a clearance.
turn: The 2020 US Customs and Border Protection award for autonomous surveillance towers, the first program where Anduril displaced an incumbent prime on delivered hardware rather than a study contract.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time figure; Alo Yoga parent Color Image Apparel valued off roughly 2 billion dollars of 2024 revenue
did: Started Color Image Apparel in 1992 as a screen-printing and blank-garment wholesaler with childhood friend Marco DeGeorge, then launched the Alo Yoga label in 2007 and pushed it to more than 150 owned stores and roughly 2 billion dollars in revenue by 2024.
why: Owning the blanks factory first meant Alo could reorder a colourway in weeks instead of a season. That let it chase whatever Instagram and later TikTok was wearing, while Lululemon was locked into two-season design calendars and third-party mills.
obst: Fifteen years as an anonymous contract printer with no brand equity, then a 2007 launch into a category Lululemon already owned; the company also had to build its own retail after wholesale partners refused premium shelf space to an unknown label.
turn: The 2020 pivot to celebrity and influencer gifting plus owned stores on high-rent streets, which converted Alo from a wholesale label into a brand people sought out by name.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time figure; equal co-ownership of Color Image Apparel with Danny Harris
did: Co-founded Color Image Apparel with Danny Harris in 1992, running the manufacturing and supply side while the pair moved from printing other companies blanks to owning the Alo Yoga brand launched in 2007 and its worldwide store fleet.
why: Vertical control of dyeing, cutting and sewing let Alo turn a design into shipped inventory inside a few weeks, so it could price 118 dollar leggings at full margin and never discount, while competitors carried season-long inventory risk.
obst: Building an apparel manufacturer in Los Angeles through two decades of offshoring, when nearly every competitor moved cut-and-sew to Asia and domestic factories closed; the pair kept the plants and absorbed the cost disadvantage.
turn: Deciding in 2007 to stop printing other brands garments and put their own name on the product, converting a commodity factory into a brand with pricing power.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time figure; roughly 2.8 billion dollars of it reinvested show profits plus Warner Bros Discovery and WW stakes
did: Formed Harpo Productions in 1986 and took ownership of The Oprah Winfrey Show from King World, so she owned the syndication rights rather than drawing a host salary, then launched OWN in 2011 and swapped most of it to Warner Bros Discovery for shares in 2020.
why: Talk-show hosts were employees; she made herself the rights holder. Owning the negative meant every rerun, every foreign sale and every ad break paid her rather than a distributor, and 25 years of that compounded into a balance sheet.
obst: Fired from a Baltimore anchor job in 1977 and moved to a morning talk slot as a demotion; later carried a six-year Texas beef-defamation suit after a 1996 mad-cow episode, and OWN lost money for its first three years.
turn: The 1986 ownership deal with King World, which converted a hit show from a job into an asset she controlled.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time figure; TV network sales and investment portfolio
did: Bought Japanese Super Sentai footage cheaply, re-cut it with American teenage actors as Mighty Morphin Power Rangers in 1993, built Fox Family Channel with News Corp and sold it to Disney for 5.3 billion dollars in 2001, then led a 13.7 billion dollar buyout of Univision in 2007.
why: He licensed action footage that already existed in Japan and paid only for the American wraparound scenes, so a full season cost a fraction of an original US kids show. The margin on that cost gap funded a channel, and the channel is what he actually sold.
obst: Pitched Power Rangers to every US network for roughly eight years and was turned down repeatedly as too strange; earlier he had gone bankrupt as a music promoter in Israel after a tour lost money, and arrived in America with debts.
turn: Fox Kids picking up Power Rangers in 1993 after nearly a decade of rejections, which turned a cheap library trick into the top-rated kids show in America.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time figure; roughly 7.5 percent of Oaktree plus proceeds from the Brookfield purchases
did: Left TCW in 1995 with Howard Marks and four colleagues to found Oaktree in Los Angeles, ran its distressed-debt strategy through the 2001 telecom bust and the 2008 crisis, and sold 61 percent of the firm to Brookfield in 2019 for about 4.9 billion dollars.
why: Distressed debt is a capacity-constrained business where returns come from being the only buyer in a forced-seller market. Oaktree raised its funds before the dislocations, so in 2002 and 2008 it had committed capital when banks and rivals were shrinking.
obst: Walking out of TCW in 1995 meant abandoning an established platform and re-soliciting every institutional client from scratch; Oaktree then had to raise its largest-ever distressed fund in 2007 into a market that thought credit was fine.
turn: Closing a roughly 11 billion dollar distressed reserve fund in 2008 just before Lehman failed, which let Oaktree buy through the crash while peers were gated.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time figure; just over 20 percent of Snap Inc plus prior share sales
did: Built Snapchat as a Stanford product-design project in 2011 with Bobby Murphy, made disappearing photos the default, turned down a reported 3 billion dollar Facebook offer in 2013, and listed Snap on the NYSE in 2017 with non-voting public shares.
why: Every social network before it made the permanent public profile the unit of value. Making messages vanish removed the reputational cost of posting, which unlocked a volume of daily camera use that a permanent feed could never get from teenagers.
obst: A co-founder suit from Reggie Brown settled in 2014 for a reported 157.5 million dollars; leaked emails from his fraternity years surfaced the same year; Instagram Stories copied the format wholesale in 2016 and stalled Snap user growth for two years.
turn: Refusing Facebook in late 2013, which forced Snap to build its own ad stack and kept the equity that the 2017 IPO priced.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time figure; sole ownership of Fashion Nova against roughly 2 billion dollars of annual sales
did: Dropped out of Cal State Northridge, ran discount clubwear stores in LA malls, and in 2006 turned them into Fashion Nova, which posts hundreds of new styles a week made in nearby Vernon factories and sells them through paid Instagram influencers.
why: Los Angeles cut-and-sew shops let him go from a photo to shipped product in under two weeks with no minimum order, so he could test a style at low volume and reorder only winners. Zara needed three weeks and a Spanish supply chain to do the same thing.
obst: A 2020 FTC settlement of 4.2 million dollars over suppressing negative customer reviews; a 2019 Labor Department finding of wage violations at LA contractors making its clothes; and an attempted armed robbery outside his home in 2021.
turn: Paying Cardi B and a wall of micro-influencers to wear the brand from 2017, which made Fashion Nova the most-Googled fashion brand in the world in 2018 with no traditional advertising.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time figure; Skims stake marked at the 5 billion dollar valuation set in the 2025 round
did: Launched KKW Beauty in 2017, then co-founded the shapewear label Skims with Jens and Emma Grede in 2019, extending it from online-only into 20 physical stores across the US and Mexico and a 5 billion dollar valuation in a 2025 funding round.
why: Shapewear was sold as a corrective secret in beige. Skims put it in every skin tone and every size, priced it as apparel rather than underwear, and used her audience to make the launch inventory sell out before any retailer had to be persuaded to stock it.
obst: The brand launched in 2019 as Kimono and was forced into a public renaming after Kyoto officials and Japanese customers objected; Coty later wrote down most of its KKW Beauty stake, and she bought the business back into Skims in 2025.
turn: The 2019 rename and relaunch as Skims, after which the first drop sold out in minutes and proved the audience converted to purchase rather than just attention.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time figure; just over 20 percent of Snap Inc plus prior share sales
did: Wrote the original Snapchat client and server in 2011 as the technical half of the founding pair, and as CTO built the camera, Lenses augmented-reality platform and the ad-serving infrastructure that carried Snap through its 2017 NYSE listing.
why: Snapchat had to render, upload and delete media on the phones teenagers actually owned in 2012, on carrier data. Building around a camera-first client rather than a web feed made the app cheap to run and impossible to replicate as a website.
obst: The pair were sued by Reggie Brown, an excluded third founder, and settled in 2014 for a reported 157.5 million dollars; Snap also disclosed a 2014 breach of 4.6 million usernames and phone numbers through an unsecured API.
turn: Shipping Lenses in 2015, which moved Snap from a messaging utility to a camera platform and created the ad format that carried its revenue.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time figure; founder stake marked at Andurils 61 billion dollar May 2026 valuation
did: Left Palantir, where he was an early engineer and then director of engineering, to co-found Anduril in 2017 and run it as CEO, scaling it to about 8,000 staff and 2.2 billion dollars of annual revenue building autonomous aircraft, missiles and command software.
why: He applied Palantirs forward-deployed engineering model to hardware: build the product first on private capital, put engineers next to the operators, and sell a finished system. That inverted the cost-plus cycle that keeps prime contractors slow and expensive.
obst: Anduril had to win clearances, facility accreditation and program access as an unproven company while Silicon Valley investors and engineers openly refused defense work after the 2018 Project Maven walkouts at Google.
turn: The 2022 shift from surveillance towers to weapons, including the Anvil and Roadrunner interceptors, which moved Anduril from a sensor vendor into the munitions budget.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time figure; roughly 500 million dollars of career salary plus off-court equity including SpringHill and Fenway Sports Group
did: Turned endorsement deals into equity from 2003 onward, taking a stake in Beats by Dre rather than a fee, buying into Blaze Pizza and Liverpool FC through Fenway Sports Group, and building SpringHill, which sold a minority stake at a 725 million dollar valuation in 2021.
why: Athletes are normally paid a flat endorsement fee that ends with the contract. He traded fee for ownership at the point where his attention was most valuable to a young brand, so Apples 3 billion dollar Beats purchase paid him as a shareholder, not a spokesman.
obst: Signed a 90 million dollar Nike deal at 18 with no business track record and was widely expected to be spent by 25; the 2010 Decision broadcast cost him major sponsor goodwill and made him the most disliked player in the league for two seasons.
turn: Taking equity instead of cash in Beats Electronics around 2008, which converted a modest endorsement into a reported nine-figure payout when Apple bought Beats in 2014.

s: Skechers DEF 14A filed 2025: Robert Greenberg beneficially owned 17,927,384 Class A shares including 17,875,656 Class B; 3G Capital merger closed Sept 2025 at 63.00 dollars per share cash
m: Disclosed beneficial share count times the 63.00 dollar all-cash merger consideration, 17,927,384 x 63 = 1.129 billion dollars
did: Founded Skechers in Manhattan Beach in 1992 after losing control of LA Gear, built it into a 9 billion dollar revenue footwear company on comfort-first walking and work shoes, and sold it to 3G Capital in September 2025 at 63 dollars a share.
why: Nike and Adidas priced performance and chased athletes. Skechers ignored the athlete entirely and sold comfort at 60 to 90 dollars into department stores and its own outlets, a price band the sponsorship-funded brands could not defend without cutting their marketing budgets.
obst: He had already been forced out of LA Gear after its 1990s collapse and started again at 52; Skechers then took a 40 million dollar FTC settlement in 2012 over Shape-ups toning-shoe claims and fought years of Nike and adidas design-patent suits.
turn: The 2013 relaunch around performance running and memory-foam walking shoes, which broke Skechers out of the fashion-sneaker cycle and doubled revenue in four years.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time figure; Fenty Beauty joint venture with LVMH plus roughly 28 percent of Savage X Fenty
did: Launched Fenty Beauty with LVMH in 2017 with 40 foundation shades at once, then built the Savage X Fenty lingerie line, which raised 125 million dollars in 2022; Forbes credits the cosmetics venture with most of her fortune rather than her music.
why: Prestige beauty had standardised on about 20 shades because deep tones sold slowly per SKU. Launching 40 at once made the darkest shades the story rather than an afterthought, and the sell-out of those shades forced every competitor to reformulate.
obst: Her prior licensing deals in fragrance had underperformed and retail partners doubted a musician-led prestige line; the Fenty ready-to-wear house she opened with LVMH in 2019 was shut down in 2021 after two years.
turn: The September 2017 launch when the deepest foundation shades sold out first, which proved the underserved market was real and reset the industry shade standard.

s: Live Nation DEF 14A filed 24 Apr 2026: 4,417,460 shares beneficially owned as of 13 Apr 2026; LYV closed 181.82 dollars on 21 Aug 2026
m: Disclosed beneficial ownership including exercisable options and restricted stock times market close, 4,417,460 x 181.82 = 803 million dollars
did: Became CEO when Clear Channel spun off its concerts arm as Live Nation in 2005, then merged it with Ticketmaster in 2010 to combine promotion, venues and ticketing in one company that now runs more than 26 billion dollars of annual revenue.
why: Promoters made almost nothing on the ticket face; the fees went to Ticketmaster. Owning both sides let Live Nation bid above-market guarantees to lock artists into its venues and recover the money on service fees, which no standalone promoter could match.
obst: The Ticketmaster merger cleared only under a 2010 DOJ consent decree, which was extended in 2019 after findings of violations; the DOJ and 30 states then sued in May 2024 to break the company up, and the 2022 Taylor Swift onsale collapse triggered Senate hearings.
turn: The 2010 Ticketmaster merger, which converted a low-margin promotion business into a fee-collecting toll on the entire live-music market.

s: ServiceTitan DEF 14A filed 5 May 2026: 8,151,001 shares and options beneficially owned; TTAN closed 94.87 dollars on 21 Aug 2026
m: Sum of disclosed direct, family-trust, GRAT and exercisable-option holdings times market close, 8,151,001 x 94.87 = 773 million dollars
did: Co-founded ServiceTitan in Glendale in 2012 with Ara Mahdessian to give home-services contractors dispatch, invoicing and payments software, after both watched their immigrant fathers run plumbing and construction businesses on paper; the company listed on Nasdaq in December 2024.
why: Trade contractors were the last large vertical without software because each shop was too small to sell to individually. Pricing per technician and bundling payments meant revenue scaled with the contractors own growth, turning a fragmented market into one predictable ARR base.
obst: Contractors refused to buy software from two engineers with no trade background, so the founders spent the early years riding along on service calls; the company also had to survive a 2022 to 2024 private-market repricing before it could list.
turn: The December 2024 Nasdaq IPO, which validated a vertical-SaaS thesis that public investors had spent two years discounting.

s: Masimo DEF 14A filed 26 Mar 2025: Kiani beneficially owned 4,040,848 shares, 7.5 percent; Danaher acquisition closed June 2026 at 180.00 dollars per share cash
m: Disclosed beneficial share count times the 180 dollar cash merger price, 4,040,848 x 180 = 727 million dollars
did: Founded Masimo in a Laguna Hills garage in 1989 on a second mortgage of about 40,000 dollars, invented Signal Extraction Technology pulse oximetry that reads oxygen through patient motion, and built it into a device maker Danaher bought at 180 dollars a share in June 2026.
why: Conventional pulse oximeters failed exactly when patients moved or perfused poorly, so alarms were ignored. Solving motion artefact turned the reading from advisory into actionable, and hospital purchasing then had a clinical reason to displace an entrenched Nellcor install base.
obst: Nellcor and its parent locked Masimo out of hospital group purchasing contracts for a decade; Masimo won a 2005 antitrust verdict of about 140 million dollars against Tyco, and in 2024 the activist Politan Capital took board control and Kiani lost the company he founded.
turn: The 2005 antitrust jury verdict against Tyco and Mallinckrodt, which broke the exclusive-contract blockade and finally let hospitals buy Masimo sensors.

s: Trade Desk DEF 14A filed 2026: 11,483,384 Class A and 42,071,879 Class B shares beneficially owned; TTD closed 13.18 dollars on 21 Aug 2026
m: Combined Class A and Class B beneficial ownership times market close, 53,555,263 x 13.18 = 706 million dollars, down from over 7 billion at the 2021 peak
did: Sold his first ad exchange AdECN to Microsoft in 2007, then founded The Trade Desk in Ventura in 2009 as a demand-side platform buying programmatic advertising for agencies, listed it in 2016, and pushed the industry to adopt his Unified ID identity standard.
why: Google and the exchanges sold both the inventory and the buying tool, so buyers could never tell whether they were being fairly priced. Building only the buy side, and refusing to own media, made The Trade Desk the one platform with no conflict of interest to disclose.
obst: The stock fell more than 90 percent from its 2021 high after execution failures on the Kokai platform rollout and a Q2 2026 miss, wiping out most of his paper wealth; the company also had to rebuild identity infrastructure twice as third-party cookies were deprecated.
turn: Connected TV becoming a biddable channel from 2019, which gave The Trade Desk the one large ad market where Google did not already own the inventory.

s: Forbes profile figure of 700 million dollars, published 3 June 2025 with the Americas Richest Self-Made Women list
m: Forbes published figure; Rare Beauty valued at about 1.3 billion dollars with Gomez holding at least 51 percent
did: Launched Rare Beauty in 2020 through Sephora, keeping majority ownership rather than licensing her name, and built it to roughly 370 million dollars of revenue by 2023 on a mental-health positioning and a single hero product, the Soft Pinch liquid blush.
why: Celebrity beauty lines normally license the name to an operator for a royalty. She funded and owned the company, so the enterprise value accrued to her; the anti-perfection positioning also gave the brand a reason to exist that survived her own attention cycle.
obst: She launched into a category already crowded with celebrity brands during the 2020 retail shutdown, while managing lupus and a 2017 kidney transplant; her other venture Wondermind cut 60 percent of staff in May 2025.
turn: The 2022 TikTok breakout of the Soft Pinch liquid blush, which turned a broad line into a category-defining single product and pulled the brand into permanent Sephora endcaps.

s: Forbes profile figure of 670 million dollars, published 3 June 2025 with the Americas Richest Self-Made Women list
m: Forbes published figure; roughly 540 million dollars pre-tax from the 2020 Coty sale plus a retained 44 percent stake
did: Trademarked Kylie Lip Kits at 17, launched the company in 2015 with 250,000 dollars of modelling money and an outsourced manufacturer, ran it with a handful of employees, and sold 51 percent to Coty in January 2020 for 600 million dollars.
why: She had the audience and outsourced everything else, so the company needed almost no capital or headcount. Manufacturing at Seed Beauty and selling direct meant no retailer margin, no wholesale terms and no marketing spend, which is why a tiny team produced hundreds of millions in sales.
obst: The first drops sold out in under a minute and the company could not fulfil demand for months; after the Coty sale, filings showed the business was materially smaller than the family had claimed and Forbes stripped her billionaire designation.
turn: The November 2015 first Lip Kit drop selling out in under a minute, which proved a social audience could be converted into inventory-constrained demand.

s: ServiceTitan DEF 14A filed 5 May 2026: 6,664,869 shares and options beneficially owned; TTAN closed 94.87 dollars on 21 Aug 2026
m: Sum of disclosed trust, GRAT and exercisable-option holdings times market close, 6,664,869 x 94.87 = 632 million dollars
did: Co-founded ServiceTitan in 2012 with Vahe Kuzoyan and runs it as CEO, selling dispatch, pricebook, marketing-attribution and payments software to plumbing, HVAC and electrical contractors; the company IPOd on Nasdaq in December 2024.
why: The wedge was the pricebook, not scheduling. Showing a technician good-better-best options on a tablet raised the average ticket immediately, so the software paid for itself in the first week and the contractor never churned.
obst: Neither founder had run a trade business, and early contractors would not take meetings; they also had to build payments and financing into the product to grow revenue per customer once seat growth in a fragmented market slowed.
turn: Landing large multi-location HVAC and plumbing groups from around 2018, which moved ServiceTitan from single-truck shops into private-equity-backed roll-ups with real budgets.

s: Cheesecake Factory DEF 14A filed 2026: David Overton beneficially owned 3,520,679 shares, 7.0 percent, as of 16 Mar 2026; CAKE closed 113.33 dollars on 21 Aug 2026
m: Disclosed beneficial ownership including options exercisable within 60 days times market close, 3,520,679 x 113.33 = 399 million dollars
did: Took his mothers cheesecake wholesale business and opened the first Cheesecake Factory restaurant in Beverly Hills in 1978, expanded on oversized menus and no-reservation waits, took it public in 1992 and grew it past 3.8 billion dollars of annual revenue.
why: A 250-item menu is an operational nightmare, so nobody copied it. He solved it with a central bakery, heavy prep standardisation and enormous kitchens, which let one location serve every occasion and sustain sales per unit roughly double the casual-dining average.
obst: He was a drummer with no restaurant training and the family bakery nearly failed before the first restaurant opened; the chain also carried heavy debt through the 2008 downturn and had to shut dining rooms nationwide in 2020.
turn: The 1992 IPO, which funded national expansion of a format that until then existed only in Southern California.

s: FIGS DEF 14A filed 23 Apr 2026: Catherine Spear beneficially owned 21,222,953 Class A and 5,469,161 Class B shares; FIGS closed 14.68 dollars on 21 Aug 2026
m: Combined Class A and Class B beneficial ownership times market close, 26,692,114 x 14.68 = 392 million dollars
did: Left Blackstone to co-found FIGS with Heather Hasson in 2013, selling technical medical scrubs direct to nurses and doctors online instead of through uniform shops, and took the company public on the NYSE in 2021 as the first female co-CEO pair to do so.
why: Scrubs were bought once a year from a hospital-adjacent uniform store with no brand and no fit. Selling direct let FIGS charge apparel prices for antimicrobial four-way-stretch fabric and build repeat purchase, capturing a margin the uniform distributors never had.
obst: They raised the first money themselves after investors dismissed scrubs as a commodity; the stock then fell more than 80 percent from its 2021 IPO price through 2023 as pandemic demand normalised, and both founders faced a short-seller campaign.
turn: The 2021 NYSE listing at a roughly 4.5 billion dollar valuation, which proved a category everyone had written off as commodity uniforms could carry brand economics.

s: Procore DEF 14A filed 24 Apr 2026: Craig F. Courtemanche Jr. beneficially owned 6,024,423 shares, 4.0 percent; PCOR closed 63.49 dollars on 21 Aug 2026
m: Disclosed beneficial ownership including trust holdings times market close, 6,024,423 x 63.49 = 383 million dollars
did: Founded Procore in 2002 from his Santa Barbara home after building a house and finding project management ran on faxes, sold cloud construction software to general contractors for nearly two decades, and listed it on the NYSE in 2021.
why: He priced per project instead of per seat, so a contractor could put every subcontractor, architect and owner on the platform for free. That made the general contractor the distribution channel and turned each project into an unpaid sales motion into the rest of the industry.
obst: Nine years of near-zero traction before meaningful venture funding, through a construction depression that killed the customer base after 2008; the company also stayed unprofitable for more than two decades before posting its first GAAP operating profit in 2026.
turn: Switching from seat-based to unlimited-user project pricing around 2014, which removed the reason contractors kept subcontractors off the system.

s: Forbes profile figure of 360 million dollars, published 3 June 2025
m: Forbes published figure; anchored on the roughly 225 million dollar September 2023 catalogue sale to Litmus Music plus American Idol earnings
did: Sold her master recording and publishing rights in five albums to Litmus Music, backed by Carlyle, for about 225 million dollars in September 2023, after earning roughly 25 million a year as an American Idol judge and launching the non-alcoholic aperitif brand De Soi.
why: Streaming turned back-catalogue pop into a bond-like annuity with observable cash flows, so private-credit buyers would pay 20-plus times annual royalties in 2023. Selling at that multiple converted a decaying royalty stream into principal at the top of the rate cycle.
obst: Dropped by two labels before her first hit and spent years writing for other artists; she later spent nearly a decade in litigation over Dark Horse, losing a 2.8 million dollar jury verdict in 2019 before it was overturned on appeal.
turn: The September 2023 Litmus deal, which crystallised two decades of royalties into cash before streaming multiples compressed.

s: Forbes profile figure of 355 million dollars, published 3 June 2025
m: Forbes published figure; traces to the 500 million dollar 2014 L Oreal purchase of NYX, which she owned outright, plus later real-estate holdings
did: Emigrated from Korea at 13, worked in her parents beauty-supply stores, and at 25 launched NYX Cosmetics in 1999 with 250,000 dollars from her family, selling 1.99 dollar eye and lip pencils; L Oreal bought the company for about 500 million dollars in 2014.
why: She sold through beauty-supply wholesalers rather than department stores, so NYX reached the same shopper as prestige brands at a tenth of the price with no counter staff, no gift-with-purchase and no advertising. She took no outside investment, so the whole exit was hers.
obst: She built the company without venture capital or a bank line while competing against Loreal and Coty budgets; her later venture Perverse Sunglasses failed, and she restarted with Bespoke Beauty Brands in 2019.
turn: YouTube beauty tutorials from around 2010 recommending NYX as the dupe for prestige products, which created national demand her wholesale channel could suddenly fill.

s: Forbes profile figure of 298 million dollars, dated 30 December 2025
m: Forbes published figure; ahead of the disclosed roughly 1 billion dollar convertible-debt deal with Lyric Capital over his catalogue
did: Uploaded anonymous mixtapes as The Weeknd in 2010, kept ownership through his XO imprint rather than signing a standard label deal, and in late 2025 structured an approximately 1 billion dollar convertible-debt transaction with Lyric Capital against his catalogue while retiring the stage name.
why: He built demand anonymously before any label was involved, so he signed from a position where he could keep masters and imprint control. Financing the catalogue with convertible debt instead of selling it kept the upside while extracting the cash a sale would have paid.
obst: He was homeless in Toronto at 17 and released the first mixtapes with no name attached and no industry contacts; he later boycotted the Grammys entirely in 2021 after After Hours was shut out of nominations.
turn: The 2015 crossover of Cant Feel My Face and The Hills, which moved him from an alternative-R and B cult act to a mainstream pop asset with catalogue value.

s: Rivian DEF 14A filed 27 Apr 2026: 10,798,921 Class A and 3,912,500 Class B shares beneficially owned as of 23 Apr 2026; RIVN closed 16.97 dollars on 21 Aug 2026
m: Combined Class A and Class B beneficial ownership times market close, 14,711,421 x 16.97 = 250 million dollars
did: Founded Rivian in 2009 straight out of an MIT doctorate, spent a decade in stealth before revealing the R1T pickup and R1S SUV in 2018, took Amazon and Ford money, listed on Nasdaq in 2021, and moved the company headquarters to Irvine.
why: Tesla had taken sedans, so he built the two body styles American buyers actually pay premiums for and pre-sold a 100,000-van fleet order to Amazon. That commercial contract underwrote the factory and gave the consumer trucks a manufacturing base they could not have funded alone.
obst: Rivian burned roughly 1.5 billion dollars a quarter through 2022, saw its share price fall more than 80 percent from the IPO, cut staff repeatedly, and had to renegotiate the Amazon exclusivity before its R2 platform reached production.
turn: The 2019 Amazon order for 100,000 electric delivery vans, which converted a decade-old stealth company into a funded manufacturer.

s: Neurocrine Biosciences DEF 14A filed 2026: Kevin C. Gorman Ph.D. beneficially owned 1,572,104 shares, 1.5 percent, as of 31 Mar 2026; NBIX closed 152.57 dollars on 21 Aug 2026
m: Disclosed beneficial ownership including options exercisable within 60 days times market close, 1,572,104 x 152.57 = 240 million dollars
did: Co-founded Neurocrine in San Diego in 1992, ran it as CEO from 2008 to 2024, and brought Ingrezza for tardive dyskinesia to FDA approval in 2017, taking the company from a near-death shell to more than 3.3 billion dollars in annual revenue.
why: He rebuilt the company around a mechanism, VMAT2 inhibition, that had a defined patient population psychiatrists could identify from a symptom they already saw. That made a specialty sales force of a few hundred sufficient, so Neurocrine kept US rights instead of partnering the drug away.
obst: The 2006 FDA rejection of the insomnia drug indiplon destroyed the partnership with Pfizer, wiped out most of the market value and forced layoffs of roughly two-thirds of staff; he took over as CEO in 2008 with the company still rebuilding.
turn: The April 2017 FDA approval of Ingrezza, the first drug ever approved for tardive dyskinesia, which arrived eleven years after the indiplon failure.

s: Crinetics Pharmaceuticals DEF 14A filed 29 Apr 2026: R. Scott Struthers Ph.D. beneficially owned 2,578,188 shares, 2.4 percent; CRNX closed 84.69 dollars on 21 Aug 2026
m: Disclosed beneficial ownership including options exercisable within 60 days times market close, 2,578,188 x 84.69 = 218 million dollars
did: Left Neurocrine after fifteen years as a peptide chemist to found Crinetics in San Diego in 2008, building oral small-molecule replacements for the injected peptide drugs used in acromegaly and other endocrine disorders, and took it public in 2018.
why: Endocrine patients were on monthly injections because the hormones themselves are peptides. Making orally available small molecules that hit the same receptors converted a depot-injection market into a pill market, which changes both the patient population and the price a payer will accept.
obst: He started the company at 46 in the middle of the 2008 financial crisis when biotech venture funding collapsed, and Crinetics ran on grants and small rounds for years before its 2018 IPO; a competing oral programme also reached the market first.
turn: Positive late-stage acromegaly data for paltusotine around 2023 to 2024, which repriced the company from a preclinical chemistry shop into a commercial-stage endocrine franchise.

s: FIGS DEF 14A filed 23 Apr 2026: Heather Hasson beneficially owned 11,535,991 Class A and 2,814,480 Class B shares; FIGS closed 14.68 dollars on 21 Aug 2026
m: Combined Class A and Class B beneficial ownership times market close, 14,350,471 x 14.68 = 211 million dollars
did: Co-founded FIGS in 2013 after watching a nurse friend buy ill-fitting scrubs from a strip-mall uniform shop, designed the antimicrobial four-way-stretch fabric line herself, and served as co-CEO through the 2021 NYSE listing.
why: Uniform buying was a distributor relationship, not a consumer one, so no brand had ever asked a nurse what she wanted to wear for a twelve-hour shift. Designing for that shift and selling direct created repeat purchase in a category that had been annual and price-only.
obst: The founders sold scrubs out of car trunks at hospitals for the first two years because no distributor would carry them; the stock then lost most of its value after the 2021 IPO as pandemic-era hiring normalised.
turn: The 2017 shift from selling to hospital procurement to selling directly to individual clinicians online, which unlocked repeat purchase and brand pricing.

s: Live Nation DEF 14A filed 24 Apr 2026: 1,034,234 shares beneficially owned including options and restricted stock; LYV closed 181.82 dollars on 21 Aug 2026
m: Disclosed beneficial ownership times market close, 1,034,234 x 181.82 = 188 million dollars
did: Joined Live Nation as chief operating officer in April 2011, a year after the Ticketmaster merger, and rebuilt Ticketmaster technology and the sponsorship business before becoming president and CFO of a company now running more than 26 billion dollars of revenue.
why: He made the ticketing platform the data layer under the concerts business, so Live Nation could sell sponsorship and advertising priced off fan purchase history rather than venue footfall. That turned ticketing from a fee collector into the highest-margin segment.
obst: He testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee in January 2023 after the Taylor Swift Eras onsale collapsed under bot traffic, and has run the company through the DOJ and 30-state antitrust suit filed in May 2024 seeking to unwind the Ticketmaster merger.
turn: The 2018 replatforming of Ticketmaster onto a modern verified-fan and dynamic-pricing stack, which raised yield per ticket across the entire venue portfolio.

s: Douglas Emmett DEF 14A filed 2026: Jordan L. Kaplan beneficially owned 12,577,268 shares and OP units, 7.1 percent; DEI closed 11.79 dollars on 21 Aug 2026
m: Disclosed beneficial ownership including 8,888,647 operating-partnership units times market close, 12,577,268 x 11.79 = 148 million dollars
did: Joined Dan Emmetts Los Angeles property partnership in 1986, rolled up dozens of private partnerships into a REIT and took Douglas Emmett public in 2006, concentrating ownership in Westside LA and Honolulu office towers and apartments as chairman and CEO.
why: He bought only in submarkets where the coastal commission, height limits and slow-growth politics made new supply effectively illegal. Owning roughly a third of the office stock in Brentwood, Santa Monica and Century City meant rents were set by scarcity, not by construction cost.
obst: Consolidating scores of individual 1970s and 1980s partnerships into a single REIT required unanimous-ish consent from thousands of legacy investors; the office portfolio then lost more than 70 percent of its share value after 2020 as Los Angeles office occupancy collapsed.
turn: The October 2006 IPO, then the largest US REIT offering of its year, which converted an illiquid partnership stack into permanent public capital.

s: ResMed DEF 14A: Michael Farrell beneficially owned 611,640 shares as of 23 Sept 2025 including options and RSUs; RMD closed 231.52 dollars on 21 Aug 2026
m: Disclosed beneficial ownership times market close, 611,640 x 231.52 = 142 million dollars
did: Joined ResMed in 2000, ran the Americas business, and as CEO from 2013 converted a sleep-apnoea device maker into a connected-health company by putting cellular chips in every CPAP machine and building the AirView cloud, reaching 5.65 billion dollars of fiscal 2026 revenue.
why: US payers reimburse CPAP only if the patient actually uses it. Putting a modem in every device let ResMed prove compliance automatically, which made its machines the ones home-medical-equipment dealers could bill for, and locked competitors out of the reimbursement workflow.
obst: He took over a company founded by his father and had to prove independence to investors; the business then faced the 2023 GLP-1 scare, when weight-loss drugs were expected to shrink the sleep-apnoea population and the stock fell roughly 40 percent.
turn: The 2021 Philips Respironics recall of millions of CPAP devices, which handed ResMed several years of uncontested share gain in its core market.

s: Douglas Emmett DEF 14A filed 2026: Kenneth M. Panzer beneficially owned 9,863,381 shares and OP units, 5.6 percent; DEI closed 11.79 dollars on 21 Aug 2026
m: Disclosed beneficial ownership including 8,293,965 operating-partnership units times market close, 9,863,381 x 11.79 = 116 million dollars
did: Joined the Douglas Emmett partnerships in 1984 and built the operating side, running leasing, construction and property management across roughly 18 million square feet of Westside Los Angeles and Honolulu office and apartment space as president and COO.
why: Douglas Emmett leases to small professional tenants averaging a few thousand square feet, so no single departure moves the portfolio. Running its own construction and management in-house made those hundreds of small deals economic, which is why larger landlords never competed for that tenant base.
obst: Built an operating platform for thousands of small tenants through the 1990s Los Angeles recession, when aerospace layoffs emptied Westside offices; the portfolio was hit again after 2020 as remote work cut demand and the share price fell by roughly three quarters.
turn: The 2006 REIT conversion, which gave the operating platform permanent capital and let it buy through the 2009 downturn instead of refinancing through it.
